nameStory: Actinastrum gets its name from the Greek words 'aktinos' meaning ray and 'astron' meaning star, describing how these tiny algae arrange themselves in beautiful star-like clusters. The species name 'hantzschii' honors Carl August Hantzsch, a 19th-century German botanist who studied microscopic freshwater life. While it sounds like a plant name, this is actually a single-celled algae that forms distinctive radiating colonies.
description: Actinastrum hantzschii is a microscopic freshwater algae that forms distinctive star-shaped colonies visible only under magnification. Each colony consists of 4-16 individual cells arranged in a radiating pattern, like spokes on a wheel. The entire colony measures just 20-50 micrometers across - far too small to see with the naked eye. This green algae lives suspended in the water column of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.

idTips.label: Colony shape
idTips.description: Forms perfect star or wheel-like arrangements when viewed under a microscope, with individual cells radiating outward from a central point like bicycle spokes

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Individual cells are elongated and triangular, tapering from a wide base to pointed tips that extend outward from the colony center

idTips.label: Colony size
idTips.description: Entire colonies measure 20-50 micrometers across - about half the width of a human hair

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green color typical of chlorophyll-containing algae, visible as a greenish tint in water samples

idTips.label: Cell count
idTips.description: Colonies typically contain 4-16 individual cells, most commonly 8 cells arranged in perfect radial symmetry

habitat: Found in freshwater environments including ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and is often found in association with other planktonic algae. Most abundant in warmer, shallow waters where sunlight can penetrate for photosynthesis.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase, though individuals require microscopic examination to observe.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when nutrients and sunlight are optimal for growth and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into fall but begin declining as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or absent during winter months when water temperatures are too cold for active growth.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Actinastrum colonies demonstrate perfect mathematical precision - they consistently arrange their cells in precise radial symmetry that would make any architect envious, creating living geometric art in every drop of pond water.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other star-forming algae like Pediastrum, but Actinastrum's cells are distinctly triangular and taper to sharp points, while Pediastrum cells are more rounded and often have gaps between them in the colony.
contextualKnowledge: Though called by a scientific name that sounds like a flowering plant, this is actually a single-celled algae that belongs to the same group as pond scum and green water blooms. Its beauty can only be appreciated through microscopic observation, representing the hidden geometric artistry present in every natural water body.
compareHints: As the only Actinastrum species commonly found in New England waters, it's most similar to other star-forming green algae in the Chlorellaceae family. However, its distinctive triangular cell shape and perfect radial arrangement set it apart from rounder, more loosely arranged relatives like Pediastrum or Coelastrum species.
